story: ShareGPT: Share your ChatGPT conversations with one click
text: Watermarking. From an outsiders perspective, the issue appears to reaching consensus on how this can be implemented (but not in the technical sense). There's a game theoretic challenge in that if models define and publish detection mechanisms, this creates a motivation for people to use other systems that don't include this. On the technical front there's a good paper here: [LINK] , and a nice very approachable video explaining it here: [VIDEO] .

I've heard one idea of adding weights to words. The idea being if I someone hands in a essay with a higher frequency of certain words, there is a very good chance its come from a language model. [VIDEO] I'm not sure this helps with coding though, maybe variable names?

story: Research shows we can only accurately identify AI writers about 50% of the time
text: I think watermarking is a better solution. There is a paper on it: Kirchenbauer, J., Geiping, J., Wen, Y., Katz, J., Miers, I., & Goldstein, T. (2023). A watermark for large language models. arXiv preprint arXiv:2301.10226. ( [LINK] ) Also, Computerphile did a video on it: [VIDEO] But of course, watermarking or your proposed solution (checksums) only work while the general public cannot run a tool like ChatGPT locally on personal computers. And it's only a matter of time before that happens. So in the long run, we need to either: 1. take away control from the users over their personal computers, in the form of what I would call 'AI DRM' (I strongly oppose this option), or 2. legislate: enforce a legal obligation to disclose that a text is not created by a human, or 3. accept that we cannot know whether or not a text is written by a human, and work with that reality

story: GPT detectors are biased against non-native English writers
text: There's an interesting scheme described here: [VIDEO] Essentially by biasing the LLM's token choices slightly you can infer with high probability later that the text was generated by it.
